To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the diffraction limited image of a collimated laser beam is ∼2 &mgr;m, that the aberration of the eye causes the image to increase in size to about 10 &mgr;m for a 2 mm pupil, and that the image size can be as small as 2 &mgr;m for eyes with small aberrations.
the retinal damage threshold, EDx, for a 532-nm laser beam incident on the cornea of the human eye is reduced from 0.5 J/cm2 to 0.2 J/cm2 when the pupil size is reduced from 6 mm to 2 mm.
the effects of ocular aberrations on the retinal image size are significant and that the effects of aberrations on the laser damage thresholds are also significant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of optical aberrations in the human eye on the retinal hazard of lasers.
the effects of ocular aberrations on the retinal damage thresholds in the human eye.
the effects of ocular aberrations on retinal damage thresholds for exposures of the human eye to laser radiation in the thermal confinement (exposure times < 10 &mgr;sec) regime.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no significant differences in retinal damage thresholds between eyes with normal ocular aberrations, or eyes with aberrations that have been corrected by laser eye surgery.

, for the thermal confinement regime, the retinal damage threshold, EDx, is a function of pupil diameter and that, for any given exposure time, the most vulnerable eyes are those with pupil sizes of 2–3mm.
, for a given exposure duration, the retinal damage threshold is inversely proportional to the square of the pupil diameter, and is also a function of the eye's ocular aberrations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the thermal confinement limit, retinal damage threshold exposures in the human eye will be significantly higher for large pupils (6 mm) than for small ones (2–3 mm).

the ocular aberrations of the human eye are not a negligible factor in determining the retinal hazard from a collimated laser beam, and that the effects of aberrations should be considered when setting laser safety limits.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a diffraction limited retina to estimate retinal damage thresholds is not justified for exposures of less than 10 &mgr;sec.
the effects of aberrations are significant and should be considered in setting safety limits for retinal exposure to optical radiation.
the retinal hazard of a given exposure depends on the pupil diameter, which is determined by the ambient light conditions.
